articles.headline: Extreme Networks, Inc. Settles with OFAC for Sanctions Violations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Extreme Networks, Inc. on October 27, 2026. The settlement addresses apparent violations of various sanctions programs administered by OFAC.

Details of the violations and the terms of the settlement were not immediately released in the initial announcement, but such agreements typically involve a monetary penalty and commitments from the company to enhance its sanctions compliance program.

This action underscores OFAC's continued enforcement efforts across a range of sanctions programs, emphasizing the importance for companies to maintain robust compliance frameworks to prevent unauthorized transactions.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends FAQs on Blocking, Rejecting Transactions, and Reporting Requirements
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued amended Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) on October 26, 2026, providing updated guidance on blocking and rejecting transactions, as well as filing reports with OFAC.

These amendments aim to clarify existing regulations and assist financial institutions and other entities in complying with their sanctions obligations. The updated FAQs often address common compliance challenges and provide practical interpretations of OFAC's rules.
The issuance of amended FAQs is a regular practice by OFAC to ensure that its guidance remains current and responsive to evolving sanctions landscapes and industry inquiries.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Iran-related Designations, Belarus and North Korea Removals, and New General Licenses
body: On October 21, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations, alongside removals of designations related to Belarus and North Korea. The action also included the issuance of new Iran-related and Russia-related General Licenses and amended Frequently Asked Questions.

The Iran-related designations are part of ongoing efforts to pressure the Iranian regime, particularly under "Operation Economic Outcast," which targets various sectors of Iran's economy and financial system.

The removals for Belarus and North Korea, while not detailed in the initial announcement, suggest specific entities or individuals previously sanctioned no longer meet the criteria for designation. The new General Licenses for Iran and Russia aim to authorize certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited, providing specific carve-outs for humanitarian aid or other policy-driven activities.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements PAIPA Designations and Associated General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA) on October 19, 2026. These designations are accompanied by the issuance of associated General Licenses.

PAIPA aims to combat the theft of American intellectual property and impose sanctions on individuals and entities involved in such illicit activities. The designations target those deemed to be undermining U.S. economic security through intellectual property theft.

The accompanying General Licenses are intended to mitigate any unintended consequences of the designations, allowing for certain transactions or activities to proceed that would otherwise be prohibited.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-related General License and FAQ
body: On October 16, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and a corresponding Frequently Asked Question (FAQ). This action reflects ongoing adjustments to U.S. sanctions policy concerning Venezuela.

The amendment to the General License likely modifies the scope of authorized transactions or activities related to Venezuela, potentially easing or tightening restrictions in specific areas. These changes are often made in response to evolving political or humanitarian conditions in the country.
The updated FAQ provides clarification on the amended General License, helping individuals and entities understand their compliance obligations and the permissible scope of engagement with Venezuela.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iran-related and Cuba-related Entities, Issues New General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related and Cuba-related designations on October 15, 2026. This action also included the issuance of new and amended General Licenses and Frequently Asked Questions.
The Iran-related designations are part of the U.S. government's continued pressure campaign against the Iranian regime, targeting entities involved in various illicit activities.

The Cuba designation and associated General Licenses reflect the ongoing implementation of Executive Order 14404, which imposes sanctions on those responsible for repression in Cuba and threats to U.S. national security.

articles.headline: OFAC Removes Venezuela-related Designation
body: On October 14, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the removal of a Venezuela-related designation. This action signifies a change in the U.S. sanctions list concerning individuals or entities associated with Venezuela.

Specifically, Jorge Rodriguez, the head of Venezuela's National Assembly, was removed from OFAC's Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) list. This delisting ends the associated asset freeze and removes obstacles for U.S. persons seeking to engage with him.
This move comes amid a broader U.S. push for diplomacy and expanded energy investment in Venezuela, signaling a potential shift in Washington's sanctions policy towards the South American nation.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations on October 13, 2026. These designations target individuals and entities involved in illicit drug trafficking and terrorist financing activities globally.

These actions are part of the U.S. government's ongoing efforts to disrupt and dismantle criminal networks that pose a threat to international security and stability. The designations typically result in asset freezes and prohibitions on transactions with the designated parties.
Such designations underscore the U.S. commitment to combating global illicit finance and preventing these networks from accessing the international financial system.

articles.headline: Bank of America Settles with OFAC for Sanctions Violations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Bank of America, N.A. on October 13, 2026. The settlement addresses apparent violations of various sanctions programs administered by OFAC.
The settlement amount for Bank of America was $11,662,930, addressing 475 apparent violations of sanctions programs targeting Russia, Belarus, Iran, Burma, Somalia, narcotics, and global terrorism.

This enforcement action highlights OFAC's continued focus on ensuring that financial institutions maintain robust compliance programs to prevent sanctions breaches across a broad spectrum of prohibited activities.

articles.headline: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics Settles with OFAC; ICC Designation and Burma Removal
body: On October 9, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics. Concurrently, OFAC announced an International Criminal Court (ICC) designation and a Burma-related designation removal, along with associated General Licenses.

The settlement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics addresses apparent violations of OFAC sanctions regulations. The specific details of the violations and the settlement terms were not immediately provided in the initial announcement.

The ICC designation and Burma-related removal reflect targeted adjustments to U.S. sanctions policy, potentially in response to specific actions or changes in circumstances related to these entities or regions.

articles.headline: EU Adopts 22nd Sanctions Package Against Russia, Designating Nearly 1,600 Entities and Individuals
body: On October 12, 2026, the European Union adopted its 22nd package of sanctions against Russia, marking the largest single expansion of its sanctions listings since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The package adds 1,569 individuals and entities to the EU sanctions lists, comprising 826 Russian companies and 743 individuals, bringing the total number of designations under the Ukraine-related sanctions regime to almost 4,600. These measures primarily target Russia's military-industrial complex, including businesses involved in the production and supply of components for missiles, drones, and military aircraft.

The new listings also include 77 individuals involved in the illegal Russian State Duma elections held in September 2026 in occupied Ukrainian territories. This package reinforces the EU's commitment to increasing pressure on Russia in response to its continued aggression against Ukraine.

articles.headline: EU Sanctions Three Individuals and Four Entities Over DPRK Nuclear and Missile Programs
body: The Council of the European Union adopted additional restrictive measures against three individuals and four entities on October 12, 2026, under its autonomous sanctions list on the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK).

These designations target those responsible for supporting, promoting, or facilitating activities that contribute to the DPRK's programs related to nuclear weapons, ballistic missiles, or other weapons of mass destruction, as well as for violating and evading United Nations sanctions.

The new listings are linked to the growing military and economic cooperation between the DPRK and Russia, including the deployment of DPRK workers in Russia, commercial and industrial cooperation, and the 'arms-for-oil' trade, all in violation of UN Security Council prohibitions.

articles.headline: EU Renews Autonomous Sanctions Regime Against ISIL/Da'esh and Al-Qaeda Until 2027
body: The Council of the European Union renewed its autonomous restrictive measures against ISIL/Da'esh and Al-Qaeda and associated persons, groups, undertakings, and entities on October 26, 2026. The regime has been prolonged for another year, until October 31, 2027.

The autonomous list currently applies to 15 persons and 8 groups, all of whom are subject to an asset freeze and, for individuals, a travel ban to the EU. EU persons and entities are also prohibited from making funds, financial assets, or economic resources available to them.
These measures complement those imposed by the UN Security Council against ISIL/Da'esh and Al-Qaeda, underscoring the EU's commitment to countering the ongoing terrorist threat.

articles.headline: OFSI Issues General Licence INT/2026/11080040 for Russia Sanctions Wind-Down
body: On October 8, 2026, the Office of Financial Sanctions Implementation (OFSI) issued General Licence INT/2026/11080040 under Regulation 64 of The Russia (Sanctions) (EU Exit) Regulations 2019.

This General Licence permits persons to wind down from any transactions involving a Designated Person (DP) to which that person is a party. This provides a legal basis for entities to conclude existing business relationships with sanctioned individuals or entities in a controlled manner.

Entities intending to utilize this General Licence are advised to consult the full text of the Licence for complete details regarding definitions, permissions, and usage requirements to ensure compliance.

articles.headline: UN Security Council Debates Iran Sanctions Expiry and Nuclear Program Amid Worsening Tensions
body: The UN Security Council held a contentious debate on October 27, 2026, regarding the expiry status of Iran sanctions and the country's continuing nuclear program. Tensions have escalated following military strikes between the United States, Israel, and Iran earlier in the year.

Russia and China rejected the premise of the meeting, asserting that the Council concluded its consideration of the Iranian nuclear issue and terminated the "non-proliferation" agenda item on October 18, 2025, citing resolution 2231 (2015). However, France, the United Kingdom, and the United States countered that Iran's non-compliance with its safeguards obligations means resolution 2231 (2015) remains in force.

The debate highlighted the deep divisions within the Security Council regarding the interpretation of the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) and the ongoing international efforts to address Iran's nuclear activities.

articles.headline: Cuba Accuses US of Threatening Countries Ahead of UN Embargo Vote
body: Cuba has accused the United States of threatening countries with tariffs, visa restrictions, and other retaliatory measures to influence their votes on an upcoming United Nations resolution calling for an end to the long-running embargo against the island.

Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez stated on October 21, 2026, that U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Washington's ambassador to the UN, Mike Waltz, are personally leading this campaign. The UN General Assembly has historically voted overwhelmingly in favor of resolutions calling for an end to the U.S. economic embargo on Cuba, which has been in place for over six decades.

Since the beginning of 2026, the Trump administration has intensified pressure on Cuba by blocking oil supplies and threatening tariffs on countries supplying fuel, leading to severe shortages and prolonged blackouts in Cuba.

articles.headline: US Consumer Confidence Recovers in October as Inflation Expectations Decline
body: American confidence in the economy rebounded somewhat in October 2026, as gas prices eased modestly, though they remain elevated. According to Conference Board survey results, average 12-month inflation expectations among consumers declined, but remained elevated at 5.8%.

Despite declining CEO confidence in the fourth quarter, consumers still anticipate higher household incomes in six months. This suggests a divergence in sentiment between consumers and business leaders regarding the U.S. economic outlook.

Core CPI, excluding volatile food and energy costs, rose 0.3% month-over-month in September, with a year-over-year increase of 2.6%, faster than the 2.4% rise in August. Prices for recreation, used cars and trucks, education, airline fares, medical care, and apparel were higher.

articles.headline: OCC Announces Enforcement Actions for October 2026, Including Penalties for BSA Deficiencies
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) released its enforcement actions for October 2026 on October 22, 2026. These actions include a Cease and Desist Order and Civil Money Penalty against American Express National Bank, Sandy, Utah, for deficiencies in its Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) compliance program, failure to timely file suspicious activity reports, and customer due diligence and customer identification program violations.

A civil money penalty of $350 million was assessed against American Express National Bank. Additionally, Bank of America, National Association, Charlotte, North Carolina, received a civil money penalty of $750 million for similar BSA compliance program deficiencies, failure to timely file suspicious activity reports, and sending wires with inaccurate transmittor name information.

The OCC also issued Orders of Prohibition against individuals, including Jennifer Hamblin, a Vault Teller at Fifth Third Bank, N.A., for embezzling approximately $292,000, and Christopher Organista, a Former Operations Processor at U.S. Bank National Association, for embezzling approximately $194,131 in customer funds.

articles.headline: BIS Renews Temporary Denial Order Against Mahan Airways and Affiliates
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) renewed a Temporary Denial Order (TDO) against Mahan Airways, Al Naser Airlines, Ali Abdullah Alhay, and Bahar Safwa General Trading on October 26, 2026. This renewal extends the denial of export privileges for these entities.

The TDO, initially issued on October 27, 2025, prohibits these parties from participating in any transactions subject to the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). The renewal request was submitted by BIS's Office of Export Enforcement (OEE) more than 20 days before the TDO's scheduled expiration, and no opposition was received.

This action underscores BIS's ongoing efforts to prevent entities from engaging in activities contrary to U.S. national security and foreign policy interests, particularly concerning unauthorized exports and reexports.

body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing one entity from the Entity List under the destination of Turkey.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
